title: The net of views
hookLine: sixty-two views caught like fish in a fine net
last: THE GROUND THE SUMMIT STANDS ON.

cards: Is the world eternal? Did it begin by chance? Is the self the same after death?
Will it be destroyed? In the Buddha's India, wandering philosophers argued questions like these from town to town. Some are still argued over kitchen tables and on podcasts.
The first long discourse, after the small things, turns to the deep things: every theory about self and world the Buddha could name. He counts them. Sixty-two.

teach.b: They fall into two groups. Eighteen are about the past: that self and world are eternal, or partly eternal, or finite, or infinite, or arose by chance.
There are even the eel-wrigglers, who slip out of every question without committing to anything.
Forty-four are about the future: that the self survives death with perception, or without it, or is destroyed, or that the highest bliss is found right here, in pleasure or in meditation.

The Buddha describes each with care, and how people arrive at it: some through deep meditation that shows them a slice of the past, and then generalize from it; some through reasoning alone. Then the turn.
Every one of these views depends on contact, the senses meeting the world.
From contact, feeling. From feeling, craving. And from craving, clinging to a view.
The Pali word is ditthi: view, opinion, literally something seen. And the image.

teach.h: A FINE NET OVER A SMALL POND
teach.b: A skilled fisherman casts a fine-meshed net over a small pond. Whatever fish of any size are in it, they're all inside the net; when they rise, they rise inside it.
So with these sixty-two views: whoever theorizes about the past or the future is caught, however they thrash. The one who sees how views arise isn't caught.

Not because he holds a sixty-third view, but because he understands the net. Look back at the week: no excuse, yours, the middle way, the long ones, not elated, not angry, the small things. And now the net.

how: The Brahmajala Sutta is studied in Theravada monasteries as a survey of speculative views; teachers use it to show practitioners how views arise from feeling and craving rather than to promote a rival theory.

games.q: what does “the net of views” mean?
o: a list of the Buddha's own beliefs
a fishing rule from the monks' code
all sixty-two theories, caught in one net

games.q: the net of views: tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha answers the sixty-two views with a sixty-third
he shows how all views arise from contact, feeling and craving, and isn't caught by them.
some of the views come from meditation experiences that are then generalized
seeing a slice of the past and building a theory on it.
the image is a fisherman's fine net over a small pond
whatever fish rise, they rise inside the net.

games.q: a wanderer asks you: is the world eternal or not? which way does DN 1 point?
o: look at how the view arises: contact, feeling, craving.
pick the answer that feels most comforting.
count the people who believe each answer.
games.why: the discourse traces every such view back to contact, feeling and craving, and says one who understands this isn't caught in the net.

practice: Pick an opinion you hold strongly, about politics, about people, about how the world works, and don't argue for or against it; just watch where it seems to live in the body and what feeling sits under it, pleasant or tense, with wanting or without.
See it as something that arose, then rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: The net of views. Sixty-two theories of self and world, all arising from contact, feeling and craving, all held in one fine net.

orig.note: Pali ditthi (Sanskrit drishti): view, opinion, literally 'something seen'.

carryVoice: Your line: all views, in the net. Understanding the net isn't one more view inside it. Day five hundred twenty-five.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 1, Brahmajala Sutta (the supreme net)
